governing_thought: The distance between what Thailand's climate adaptation platform needs and what it currently holds is not a general shortage of data but eleven named structural gaps that combine into a different obstacle for each of the platform's eight planned services, a website content base only 21 percent ready to publish outright, and -- in its most binding and self-evident form -- a continuing international reporting obligation DCCE already holds and cannot yet compile without hand-assembled, untraceable effort; establishing the shape of this shortfall precisely, built by subtracting Chapter 3's inventory from Chapter 2's requirements, is what makes the recommendations in section 5.2 actionable rather than aspirational.

narrative_scqa.situation: Chapter 2 established what the platform's information architecture and data management framework require; Chapter 3 established what Thailand's data ecosystem, information services, and website content currently supply. This section places the two side by side.
narrative_scqa.complication: The subtraction does not yield one generic shortage. It yields eleven named structural gaps that combine differently to block each of the platform's eight planned services; a website content base where only 21 percent of required topics are publication-ready outright and 44 percent have no source at all; and, sharpest of all, DCCE's own continuing obligation to compile an international adaptation transparency report, which is blocked today not by missing raw data so much as by a compilation process with no shared definitions and no traceable calculation method.
narrative_scqa.question: How large and how structured is this shortfall, and what does it require of the platform being designed to close it?
narrative_scqa.answer: The shortfall is precise enough to act on: eleven gaps, each addressable on its own terms; a website content base whose weakest quarter needs fresh research rather than republishing; and a reporting obligation that proves, in miniature, that the platform's task is to make an existing but fragmented data ecosystem trustworthy and traceable, not to accumulate more of it. What that requires in practice -- policy, technical, and governance recommendations -- is the subject of section 5.2.

argument_units.claim: Comparing the seven forms of demand established in Chapter 2 against the 260-dataset national catalog established in Chapter 3 separates the shortfall into eleven named structural gaps, not one undifferentiated shortage of data.
argument_units.grounds:
SUPPLY-SIDE PROFILE. The national catalog holds 260 datasets. Ownership concentrates in six agencies -- Thai Meteorological Department 37, DCCE 26, GISTDA 17, Department of Disaster Prevention and Mitigation 15, National Statistical Office 14, Office of the National Economic and Social Development Council 14 -- which together hold roughly half the catalog. By subject, the catalog holds 72 vulnerability datasets, 68 exposure datasets, 49 covering the physical climate signals that drive hazard models, and 36 finished hazard products such as flood and drought maps; the remainder covers loss and damage records, composite indices, risk metrics, and spatial reference layers. About 17% is openly published and the rest is available only on request. About half the catalog is recorded as CSV, with raster, vector, and document formats making up most of the balance. On resolution, 122 datasets are held at province level, 41 at a local grain (sub-district, municipality, village, or individual monitoring point), and 36 as gridded surfaces, while for 59 datasets -- close to a quarter of the catalog -- resolution is not recorded at all, so the grain is not knowable from the catalog alone. All 260 entries carry draft status and none has completed a verification step, because that step does not yet exist as a process; this describes a stage the catalog has not reached, not the quality of the underlying data, much of which is sound. One recent addition changes the resolution picture materially: DCCE's Climate Change Research Center has produced statistically downscaled climate data at 5km resolution covering precipitation and maximum, minimum, and mean temperature under both the SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios, a substantially better foundation than the 25km grid available when this analysis was first run.

IMPORTANT READING NOTE FOR GAP 1 (do not let the prose contradict itself): the subject counts above show more vulnerability and exposure datasets than hazard-side ones by raw count. Gap 1's imbalance is therefore NOT a claim that exposure and vulnerability data is scarcer in total. It is a claim about coherence and fitness -- hazard information arrives model-ready and internally consistent, while the exposure and vulnerability holdings are scattered across many owners at mismatched resolutions and are thin precisely where infrastructure, economic assets, and social vulnerability are concerned. State the imbalance in those terms, never as a raw-count comparison.

THE ELEVEN GAPS, as named in the WP7 Gap Analysis Report of 16 August 2026, which supersedes all earlier versions of this analysis. (1) Balance between hazard, exposure, and vulnerability data -- the catalog describes hazards well, drawing on climate models, meteorological records, and satellite observation, while information describing the people, assets, and services that hazards affect is more scattered and thinner in the subdomains that matter most, particularly infrastructure, economic assets, and social vulnerability; work requiring several of these layers at once (identifying which vulnerable groups sit inside a risk area, ranking adaptation projects, assessing risk across an asset portfolio) needs that side of the catalog to grow. Even where hazard data is strong, it is mostly delivered as a single deterministic map or figure, with the probabilistic detail -- the range a projection covers, the assumptions a model rests on -- rarely exposed alongside it, which limits how safely that hazard information can be reused inside someone else's risk calculation. (2) Spatial resolution -- province-level figures support national strategy, but deciding where to build a drain or how high to set a seawall needs sub-district or asset grain; the new 5km downscaled data closes much of this at the climate-driver end, while the environmental layers needed alongside it (digital elevation models, stream and sub-basin routing) still come from several sources at resolutions that do not align with each other, and population and asset data broken down by social and economic category is not yet available at a matching grain. (3) Compatibility between spatial units -- hazard data arrives as grids, population and social data bounded by administrative areas, asset data as points and lines, and some economic data at province or regional level; without an agreed method for relating these to one another, each user converts and overlays them independently, which costs time, introduces error, and leaves results from different organizations that cannot be compared. The practical consequence is that no single scale can be served reliably: a risk figure at a given resolution needs its hazard, exposure, and vulnerability inputs all available at that resolution together, and that alignment does not yet exist for most combinations. (4) Access -- most of the catalog is available on request rather than published, driven by three causes: internal rules at data-holding agencies with no systematic cross-ministry sharing policy; personal data protection requirements, sometimes read as preventing release of an entire dataset where aggregation would resolve the concern; and limited budget and technical staffing for building and maintaining automated data connections. The effect is sharpest on work that needs current information -- impact-based warning, periodic financial analysis, risk assessment on a refresh cycle, and policy monitoring drawing on many sources. (5) Metadata standards -- there is not yet an agreed national standard covering the descriptive information that travels with a dataset: discovery metadata for finding it, technical metadata for using it, a data dictionary for interpreting its fields, and lineage for tracing where it came from; update frequency and expected lag between an event and its appearance in the data are also generally unstated. Without these a user cannot judge whether a dataset is suitable before relying on it, and which of these fields matter most for a given product's credibility is not settled either -- until metadata is named as an official, enforced requirement rather than a general expectation, its quality will keep varying by how much each data holder chooses to provide. (6) Format of products and services -- a finished information product delivers less than it could when it can only be viewed; a crop suitability map published solely through a web interface can be read on screen but cannot be taken as input to further analysis, which matters most for work that treats a product as an ingredient (financial risk assessment, conversion of climate data into engineering variables, macroeconomic impact analysis, infrastructure risk modelling, warning systems drawing several sources together). This overlaps Gap 4: a data owner who would allow a document or map to be viewed is often unwilling to release the same information as a downloadable analytical file, because a file that leaves their control is a file whose downstream use they can no longer answer for. (7) Time coverage and delay -- different uses need different time horizons: comparing risk against a stable reference needs 10 to 20 years of history, planning national infrastructure needs projections 20 to 50 years out, and warning systems need information arriving close to real time; the catalog does not yet cover all three consistently. (8) Risk methodology and data selection -- Thailand does not yet have a national approach to defining risk, nor a catalog of risk methods matched to the purposes they suit; without that guidance data can be applied outside the context it was built for, as when a single-scenario long-range projection is used directly as an engineering design value without accounting for model uncertainty, or when comparing relative risk between areas would be better served by an index-based map than by asset-level financial loss statistics. This carries a real risk of maladaptation. (9) Certification and stewardship -- no step currently exists in which a dataset is checked, endorsed, and marked as an official reference, which is why all 260 entries sit in draft; no dataset yet has a named person or office responsible for keeping it current, and there is no agreed process when a holding agency declines to share. (10) Calculation methods that do not yet exist -- distinct from Gap 8, which concerns choosing among available methods, several services need a method that has not been built: there is no agreed approach to weighing costs against benefits for a resilience investment, no standard for classifying government spending as climate-related, no accepted way to value losses avoided by an investment, and no reference library relating a hazard to the damage it typically causes. National economic planners have commissioned a university-led effort to build an economic loss and damage methodology aligned to international practice, which addresses part of this. (11) Decisions awaiting a determination -- several gaps close on a decision rather than on new data or analysis: the scope of the non-financial loss record, whether the commissioned loss methodology becomes the official calculation manual, dataset classification for licensing, whether to build on or replace the existing policy monitoring platform, where the impact-based warning service belongs on the site, and whether the catalog's recorded formats describe current delivery or an intended target.
argument_units.warrant: Because each gap names a specific, addressable shortfall rather than a general sense that more data is needed, the platform's next development phase can be planned against a concrete inventory instead of an open-ended research agenda -- this precision is what lets section 5.2's recommendations be scoped against named problems rather than a vague call for more data.
argument_units.application_to_design: Open with the demand-supply comparison method and the supply-side profile above, then present the eleven gaps as a numbered list, each with its full definition rather than only its name. Full report altitude means the technical detail the executive summary compressed belongs back in the main text here -- the probabilistic-detail point in Gap 1, the elevation and stream-routing detail in Gap 2, the three causes in Gap 4, the commissioned costing effort in Gap 10 -- not in an appendix. Observe the Gap 1 reading note above: the imbalance is about coherence and fitness, never about raw dataset counts.

argument_units.claim: Each of the platform's eight planned information services meets its own distinct combination of these eleven gaps, so a single blanket response -- collecting more data in general -- would not unblock most of them. Chapter 3 (section 3.3) already established these as eight services, not nine, with the platform's support for A-BTR compilation placed as a mechanism attached to Service 7 rather than as a service of its own; this section holds that placement and does not reopen it.
argument_units.grounds: Cross-referencing the WP7 Gap Analysis Report's gap-to-service mapping against the eight services Chapter 3 defined: Service 1, the certified climate data catalog, meets Gaps 4, 5, 6, and 9. Service 2, high-resolution spatial risk analytics, meets Gaps 1, 2, and 3. Service 3, finance and budget decision support, meets Gaps 6, 7, 8, and 10. Service 4, historical loss and damage assessment, meets Gaps 1, 3, 7, and 10. Service 5, climate design parameters, meets Gaps 2, 7, 8, and 10. Service 6, multi-hazard impact-based early warning, meets Gaps 4, 6, and 7. Service 7, adaptation monitoring and evaluation, meets Gaps 1, 3, 5, and 11 directly, and additionally carries the platform's A-BTR-compilation mechanism, which meets Gaps 5 and 10 on its own account -- WP7's separately numbered ninth service maps onto this same mechanism, not onto a ninth platform service, matching how Chapter 3 already placed it. Service 8, uncertainty governance, meets Gaps 5 and 8. No two services carry the same combination, and no single gap blocks all eight.
argument_units.warrant: Because different services fail for different structural reasons, sequencing their development requires naming each service's specific blocking combination first; an aggregate count of gaps would obscure exactly the information section 5.2 needs in order to prioritize which gap to close for which service.
argument_units.application_to_design: This unit produces the summary table only -- one row per service against the gaps that block it, using the exact Thai service names Chapter 3 section 3.3 already established, with the table title and column definitions the report's table rule requires. Service 7's row notes that it additionally carries the A-BTR mechanism (Gaps 5, 10); do not add a ninth row for it. Do not carry any service's mechanism here -- each service's mechanism and consequence is developed in its own subsection immediately following, so this unit must not duplicate that detail.

argument_units.claim: The certified climate data repository is blocked less by the volume of data available than by the absence of any step that marks a dataset as checked and official, which is a prerequisite for sharing a meaningful share of the catalog at all.
argument_units.grounds: Fragmentation was the most frequently raised difficulty across every stakeholder group consulted, and there is currently no consistent way to distinguish a checked dataset from an unchecked one. The certified catalog is planned as a system separate from DCCE's general open data service, built specifically for the sourcing and trust information that climate data requires, and currently holds a starting seed of content with its full scope still to be set. Gap 9 is the central obstacle: how datasets should be classified for licensing remains an open decision, and that classification is a prerequisite for sharing a substantial share of the catalog. Gaps 4, 5, and 6 compound it, since a repository whose contents are mostly request-only, undescribed by any agreed metadata standard, and published in view-only form cannot function as a citable reference even once certification exists.
argument_units.warrant: Because certification is what gives a dataset the standing to be cited in a funding decision or a policy, and because the licensing classification that certification depends on is a decision rather than a research task, this service is blocked at a governance step that no amount of additional data collection would clear.
argument_units.application_to_design: State the certification gap as the binding constraint, name the licensing classification as an open decision rather than an unfinished analysis, and note the separation between the certified catalog and the department's general open data service as a design fact established in Chapter 2.

argument_units.claim: High-resolution spatial risk analysis is blocked by two structural properties of the existing risk index that no additional input data can undo, compounded by the misalignment of the layers that would have to be combined with it.
argument_units.grounds: Banks assessing loan exposure and infrastructure planners both need flood depth and duration for a specific site rather than a single province-wide value. Two properties of the current risk index stand in the way. Its unit of analysis is fixed at province before the calculation begins, so a finer result cannot be recovered afterward. Its inputs are multiplied and normalized into a single score, which cannot be worked backward to the detail that went into it. Two routes forward have been identified -- extracting detail from the country's 77 provincial risk reduction plans, and reworking municipal boundary data -- and both await a decision to resource them. This service also shows how the gaps compound: even with rainfall projections in hand, a model that is coarse relative to the decision (Gap 2) and stored on a grid that cuts across administrative boundaries (Gap 3) cannot be combined with community-level vulnerability data (Gap 1), and local risk mapping does not become possible. The new 5km downscaled data materially improves the first of those three conditions and leaves the other two untouched.
argument_units.warrant: Because the index's province-level unit of analysis and its normalized single score are decisions taken before any data enters the calculation, finer results require rebuilding the method rather than sourcing better inputs -- which is why this service is a methodology problem wearing the appearance of a data problem.
argument_units.application_to_design: Explain both structural properties of the index plainly, since a reader who assumes finer data alone would solve this will misread the recommendation that follows in section 5.2. Name the two identified routes forward as awaiting a resourcing decision, and use this service as the worked example of how gaps compound.

argument_units.claim: Finance and budget decision support depends on Gap 10 more than any other service, because every calculation it would need to perform rests on a method that has not yet been built.
argument_units.grounds: Climate-resilient infrastructure costs more than historical comparisons suggest, and officials need a defensible way to explain that difference to auditors and budget reviewers. This service requires a cost-benefit method for resilience investment, a standard for classifying government spending as climate-related, an accepted way to value losses avoided by an investment, and a damage function library -- none of which exists. Records of international climate finance and technology transfer show funds moving but reveal little about the capability that resulted. Which figures would actually persuade different audiences is not yet established, so direct research with the intended users will be needed before the service can be specified.
argument_units.warrant: Because the missing element is the calculation method rather than the underlying financial or hazard data, this service cannot be unblocked by improving the catalog; it requires methodological work commissioned as work in its own right, which is why it appears in section 5.2 as a development recommendation rather than a data recommendation.
argument_units.application_to_design: Name all four missing methods explicitly, and state that which figures would persuade budget and audit audiences is itself an open research question -- the service cannot be fully specified until that is settled.

argument_units.claim: Historical loss and damage assessment has its method question partly answered by a commissioned national methodology, leaving the remaining distance in the source data itself and in four build elements that stay blocked until the methodology's official standing is settled.
argument_units.grounds: Relief and recovery spending records what was paid out, which is a different quantity from what disasters cost the economy. The commissioned national methodology noted under Gap 10 addresses the method side: focused initially on agricultural losses and running through mid-2026, it has produced a first estimate of roughly 1.62 trillion baht in cumulative loss and damage between 2006 and 2024. Whether it can also serve as the platform's official calculation manual is a strong possibility that has not been confirmed. With the method in view, the remaining distance is data. Disaster agency records capture who was affected and what relief was paid, without a monetary damage figure or a breakdown by sector and province, and with recorded zeros that may mean either that no event occurred or that no collection took place. Releasing the more detailed records raises a personal data question, since some are held at household level, and the timeline for that release is not yet known. Of the six specific figures this service needs, three have supporting data in the catalog; the other three are requests for improved accuracy, for adopting an international disclosure practice, and for stress-testing capability -- needs that no dataset alone would meet. Four elements of the finished product were recorded as blocked pending the methodology: a national economic loss database, a public dashboard of that history, a record of losses that do not appear on a balance sheet, and the calculation manual itself. Of the three loss categories in that third element -- mental health, biodiversity, and cultural heritage -- only biodiversity currently has supporting material, and the commissioned economic methodology does not extend to any of them.
argument_units.warrant: Because the recorded zeros in disaster data cannot be distinguished between a genuine absence of loss and an absence of collection, and because relief payments measure a different quantity from economic loss, this service's baseline cannot be assembled from existing records even once the methodology is confirmed -- the data question outlives the method question.
argument_units.application_to_design: Give the commissioned methodology and its first estimate, then state clearly that its standing as the official calculation manual is unconfirmed. Name the four blocked build elements and the three non-financial loss categories, noting that only biodiversity currently has material behind it. Do not resolve the open questions here; they belong to section 5.2 and to the decisions list.

argument_units.claim: Engineering design variables are absent at every resolution rather than merely too coarse, which is why this service has been set aside for the current phase.
argument_units.grounds: Design standards still rest on historical statistics that no longer describe current conditions. The variables this service needs -- rainfall intensity-duration-frequency curves adjusted for climate scenario, runoff coefficients, peak flow, temperature extremes, and wind gust -- are not held anywhere, at any grain. The general risk index serves hazard awareness rather than plot-level design, so it cannot substitute for them. Closing this gap will take a sustained working relationship with engineering specialists alongside the data work, which is why the service has been set aside for the current phase rather than partially specified.
argument_units.warrant: Because these variables must be derived through domain expertise rather than extracted from an existing dataset, this service is blocked on specialist collaboration that the platform cannot supply on its own, which is a different kind of dependency from every other service in this list and justifies deferring it explicitly rather than leaving it nominally in scope.
argument_units.application_to_design: State the deferral plainly and give the reason -- specialist derivation work, not a missing dataset. Name the specific variables so the reader understands what deferral covers.

argument_units.claim: Multi-hazard impact-based warning is the least developed of the eight, blocked by an access model that cannot deliver information on the timescale a warning requires.
argument_units.grounds: Practitioners want a warning that states what to do -- open cooling centers, estimate likely business interruption -- rather than a forecast value alone. No product exists yet, and the only related material is a static diagram showing how hazards cascade into impacts. Gaps 4 and 7 are decisive: a warning service needs automated connections to sensors, models, and operating agencies on a timescale that the current request-based access model cannot support. Where this service belongs on the site is also unsettled, since it is an operational tool rather than a page of reference material.
argument_units.warrant: Because a warning service's value depends entirely on the speed at which information reaches it, request-based access is not a slower version of the required capability but an incompatible one -- which makes this service dependent on automated data connections being built first, rather than on any content being written.
argument_units.application_to_design: State that this is the least developed service and why. Name the placement question as an open decision, and note that the existing cascade diagram is the only current material, so the reader does not assume a partial build exists.

argument_units.claim: Adaptation monitoring and evaluation is the one service where a working system already exists, which turns its central question into a decision about that system rather than an assessment of missing data -- and this same system is where Chapter 3 placed the platform's mechanism for supporting A-BTR compilation, developed in full in the next part of this section.
argument_units.grounds: A national monitoring platform already operates here, collecting manually entered progress data from eighteen agencies across the national plan's six sectors and holding a few hundred rows a year with no automated feed. The open question is whether the platform being designed builds on that system or replaces it, which is a Gap 11 decision rather than a research task. Two details about the existing system remain unclear: whether it already assesses technology readiness, and where individual project status is held, which currently appears to rest on staff knowledge rather than in the system. Comparing results across agencies is additionally limited by vulnerability data scattered on differing spatial units (Gaps 1 and 3) and by update cycles that are not stated (Gap 5). Chapter 3 established that this same eighteen-agency reporting pipeline is the mechanism the platform reuses to support DCCE's A-BTR compilation obligation, rather than building a separate reporting tool -- meeting Gaps 5 and 10 on that account, beyond the four gaps blocking the service's core monitoring function.
argument_units.warrant: Because an operating system already holds this ground, the risk here is not an empty capability but a duplicated one, and the build-or-replace decision has to be taken before requirements can be written -- which is why this service's obstacle is recorded as a pending determination rather than a technical gap. And because A-BTR compilation reuses this same pipeline rather than requiring a new one, its blocking gaps belong to this service's diagnosis, not to a service of their own.
argument_units.application_to_design: Describe the existing platform concretely -- eighteen agencies, six sectors, manual entry, a few hundred rows a year -- so the build-or-replace question reads as a real choice. Name the two unclear details as items requiring confirmation, and note that project status resting on staff knowledge is itself a finding. Close with a short bridge naming the A-BTR mechanism and its two blocking gaps, then hand off to the extended case study that follows -- do not develop the A-BTR diagnosis here.

argument_units.claim: Uncertainty management standards face a methodology and confidence gap rather than a data gap, and closing it is institutional learning work rather than a feature of another service.
argument_units.grounds: Financial institutions and infrastructure planners are cautious about using probabilistic projections in decisions that carry liability, and some currently treat a flood probability map as a certainty map. Uncertainty in a projection remains an unfamiliar concept for many intended users, and building shared institutional understanding of how to read it is work in its own right rather than something delivered incidentally alongside another service. A place for this content has already been identified on the site, so the shortfall is in the standard and the shared understanding, not in the platform's capacity to publish them.
argument_units.warrant: Because misreading a probability map as a certainty map produces confident wrong decisions rather than visible failures, this gap is more dangerous than an empty page would be, and it closes through an agreed standard for communicating confidence rather than through additional data.
argument_units.application_to_design: State that this is a methodology and shared-understanding gap explicitly, since the reader will otherwise expect a data recommendation. Use the flood-probability-read-as-certainty example, which makes the risk concrete without naming any organization.

argument_units.claim: Checked against DCCE's digital asset inventory, only 21 percent (16 of 75) of the website's required content topics are publication-ready outright, 35 percent (26) are partially populated, and 44 percent (33) have no current source at all -- together 79 percent still needing fresh research, synthesis, or drafting before the site defined in Chapter 2 can be published.
argument_units.grounds: The WP4 Content Source Gap Analysis v2 of 20 August 2026 checked all 75 sitemap-mandated content topics against DCCE's full digital asset inventory and, for pages needing structured data, against the 260-dataset catalog, yielding 16 FULL, 26 PARTIAL, and 33 GAP. The item count moved from 73 to 75 because the v9 restructuring collapsed one section into a router link, removing its three content requirements, and added five new items. This version supersedes the 10 August analysis, whose totals are carried in some earlier readings of this material and should not be used.
argument_units.warrant: Because this figure covers the whole website rather than any single service or reporting obligation, stating it before any service-specific finding corrects an assumption that DCCE already holds most of the content it needs to publish -- an assumption that would otherwise make the content recommendations in section 5.2 look disproportionate to the problem.
argument_units.application_to_design: State the three-way split as a short numbered breakdown with the 79 percent headline. The per-node breakdown across the 27 sitemap nodes stays out of the main text and is noted as available in the underlying analysis. Three findings underneath this figure follow as their own short passages; do not fold them into this paragraph.

argument_units.claim: Wherever a page promises financial support, technology transfer, and capacity building together, the financial material is reliably present and the other two are not -- a pattern that recurs on several pages independently.
argument_units.grounds: The content check found this combination repeating across pages that were drafted separately, which points to what the department actually tracks rather than to how any single page was written: financial support is recorded systematically, while technology transfer and capacity building are not captured in a form that can be published.
argument_units.warrant: Because the pattern appears on pages written independently of one another, it reflects a gap in what is recorded institutionally rather than an oversight in drafting, so closing it requires a change to what gets tracked rather than a round of content writing.
argument_units.application_to_design: State the pattern and its interpretation -- what is tracked, not how pages were written. This is a finding about institutional record-keeping and should read that way.

argument_units.claim: For raw climate science content, the underlying data exists but not in publishable form, which a check against publications alone would have missed entirely.
argument_units.grounds: Checking the publication inventory alone suggested a complete absence of climate science content. The fuller check against the dataset catalog found historical climate grids and downscaled projections that do exist -- but as restricted, unprocessed national-grid data rather than as the finished trend figures the pages describe.
argument_units.warrant: Because the distance here is processing and release rather than acquisition, this part of the content gap closes through a different kind of work from the topics that have no source at all, and treating the two as one undifferentiated backlog would misdirect effort.
argument_units.application_to_design: Make the distinction explicit: the data exists, the publishable figure does not. This matters for section 5.2's sequencing and should not be blurred into the general content gap.

argument_units.claim: Narrative and explanatory pages are in reasonable shape while pages designed as live data features have little structured material behind them, which is Gap 6 reappearing on the web layer.
argument_units.grounds: Background pages, policy summaries, and case studies are comparatively well supported. Pages designed as dashboards, maps, and calculators have little structured material behind them -- including pages counted as partially covered only because a document discusses the topic in prose, without the underlying data that would make the feature work.
argument_units.warrant: Because a page counted as partially covered on the strength of a prose document cannot actually be built as a dashboard or a calculator, the readiness figure understates the distance for exactly the pages that carry the platform's distinctive value, and the same view-only limitation that constrains the data layer reappears here.
argument_units.application_to_design: Name this as the same structural gap appearing on the web layer rather than as a separate finding, so the reader sees one problem with two faces. Note the counting caveat, since it qualifies the headline figure stated above.

argument_units.claim: A-BTR compilation is a continuing institutional obligation DCCE itself holds, flowing from its role as Thailand's national focal point for climate adaptation. Chapter 3 already placed the platform's support for it as a mechanism attached to Service 7 rather than a service of its own; this part of the section develops that mechanism in full, as the sharpest, most binding instance of the structural and content gaps just established.
argument_units.grounds: Thailand's own BTR2 second interim report, institutional baseline: the report must identify the principal national policy and institutional framework for adaptation including the lead national committee and the National Adaptation Plan; must describe the institutional arrangement for adaptation across policy formulation, planning, implementation, monitoring, and reporting, with clear allocation of roles and responsibilities; must identify the national focal point for adaptation and describe coordination across sectors and governance levels; and must describe how DCCE and sectoral focal points coordinate monitoring, evaluation, and regular progress reporting. The same report separately identifies DCCE as the national focal point coordinating adaptation policy formulation, inter-agency coordination, and reporting, implementing measures under the National Adaptation Plan in collaboration with sectoral ministries, provincial and local authorities, academic institutions, and development partners.
argument_units.warrant: Because these are DCCE's own reporting duties stated in the report's own institutional baseline rather than requests routed through DCCE from an outside party, justifying platform support for A-BTR does not rest on demonstrated external demand the way the other eight services do; it rests on an obligation DCCE must fulfil regardless of demand, which is why it is the platform's most binding proof case rather than one more service among eight.
argument_units.application_to_design: Open this part of the section by naming A-BTR's institutional status before describing any gap, so the platform's role reads as serving DCCE's own continuing duty. Note in one sentence that this elaborates on the Service 7 mechanism named just above, per Chapter 3 -- not a new service. State directly why the case is developed at length: it draws on the same structural and content gaps already established, in their most acute form.

argument_units.claim: Thailand's own BTR2 second interim report groups its adaptation barriers into four themes -- data and knowledge, institutional and coordination, financial and resource, and implementation, reporting, and monitoring and evaluation -- and names five specific data and knowledge gaps it identifies as currently blocking adequate reporting.
argument_units.grounds: The report's barriers section organizes its findings into those four thematic groups; this section develops the data and knowledge theme, which is where the platform's remit lies, and does not extend into the other three. Within that theme the report states five gaps and the support each would require. First, limitations in area-based risk and vulnerability data -- insufficient spatial resolution, timeliness, and coverage for vulnerable groups, sector-specific risks, and socio-economic conditions -- which cause adaptation planning to rely on generalized rather than location-specific interventions and risk maladaptation; the support named is high-resolution area-based datasets, local data collection systems, and local-agency capacity building. Second, the absence of a standardized framework, methodologies, and integrated information system for Loss and Damage assessment, with data dispersed across agencies producing methodological inconsistency, limited interoperability, and difficulty generating comprehensive assessments of economic and non-economic loss. Third, the absence of standardized outcome indicators, with monitoring relying mainly on output measures such as the number of activities carried out, which limits assessment of resilience, vulnerability reduction, adaptive capacity, national aggregation, and alignment with the Global Goal on Adaptation. Fourth, fragmentation of climate-related databases across agencies with no centralized integration platform; the support named is an integrated national climate data platform with interoperable systems, data-sharing protocols, and the legal or institutional frameworks for inter-agency exchange. Fifth, limited translation of available scientific knowledge into practical and operational tools, especially at provincial and local level, contributing to reactive rather than proactive adaptation; the support named is practical toolkits, guidelines, decision-support tools, and training.
argument_units.warrant: Because these gaps are stated by the report's own authors as the barriers currently preventing adequate reporting, they carry the standing of the country's own acknowledged baseline rather than an outside critique -- closing them addresses what the report itself says is missing, not an improvement agenda the platform invents on its own authority.
argument_units.application_to_design: Name the four thematic groups in one sentence and state plainly that this section develops the data and knowledge theme only, so the scope boundary is visible rather than silent. Then present the five gaps as a numbered list with their named support requirements. Do not propose the platform's response yet; that belongs to the concluding unit.

argument_units.claim: Beyond the content gaps BTR2 names about itself, compiling the report today is a broken process resting on four structural conditions, none of which is a shortage of raw data.
argument_units.grounds: Producing Thailand's international adaptation report currently means compiling figures by hand from spreadsheets held across several agencies, without a shared definition of terms such as avoided loss or adaptation coverage, and with final figures difficult to trace back to source. Four structural conditions sit underneath this: gaps in the underlying data and in shared definitions; coordination across the agencies holding each piece; resourcing for the compilation work itself; and a consistent means of monitoring progress between reporting rounds.
argument_units.warrant: Because a figure that cannot be traced to its source cannot be defended when questioned, and because the same term means different things to different contributing agencies, the compilation problem persists independently of how much data the catalog holds -- which is why it is described here as a process failure rather than a data shortage.
argument_units.application_to_design: State the four structural conditions as the frame for the two findings that follow. Keep the hand-compilation description concrete -- spreadsheets across agencies, no shared definitions, figures that cannot be traced -- without naming any individual agency as at fault.

argument_units.claim: Checked item by item against the catalog, roughly half of the 122 information items the report requires return no supporting data at all.
argument_units.grounds: The information the report needs was broken into 122 individual items and checked against the 260-dataset catalog. Roughly half have supporting data, some ready to use and some needing further work. Roughly half return nothing. Six items need a judgment rather than a search, the most consequential being whether a dataset DCCE already maintains is the same measure that the reporting framework refers to under a different name.
argument_units.warrant: Because the check was made against actual reporting items rather than against a general impression of coverage, the resulting figure states the reporting gap in terms that can be worked through one item at a time, and the six judgment calls identify where a decision rather than a data search would close the gap fastest.
argument_units.application_to_design: Give the 122-item figure, the roughly-half result, and the six judgment calls. Name the most consequential judgment call -- the same measure under a different name -- since it illustrates why shared definitions are load-bearing rather than administrative.

argument_units.claim: Where the unmatched items concentrate is the more useful finding: raw hazard data is rarely the missing piece, and what is missing is the calculated figure the report cites.
argument_units.grounds: The unmatched items cluster around figures that must be derived rather than measured -- return periods, scenario-specific probabilities, the loss and damage assessment methodology international reporting expects, and financial stress test results. The ingredients for these are often present in the catalog; the method that turns them into a reportable number is Gap 10.
argument_units.warrant: Because the shortfall sits in derivation rather than measurement, an investment in collecting more data would leave the reporting obligation exactly as blocked as it is today -- which is the single most consequential correction this section makes to an intuitive reading of the problem.
argument_units.application_to_design: State this as the section's sharpest finding about A-BTR. Name the four kinds of missing calculated figure, and connect the conclusion back to Gap 10 explicitly so the reader sees the structural gap and the reporting obligation as one problem.

argument_units.claim: A-BTR reporting is strategically significant precisely because it is complex to deliver: assembling the report requires that data domains and pipelines spanning all four stages of the adaptation cycle -- climate science, impact and vulnerability and risk assessment, adaptation planning and implementation, and monitoring, evaluation and learning -- are functional and consistently high quality, which is why a data platform, not a single dataset or content page, is the necessary supporting infrastructure.
argument_units.grounds: The information architecture established in Chapter 2 structures platform content around exactly these four adaptation-cycle stages. Read together with the institutional finding that A-BTR reporting spans planning, implementation, monitoring, and reporting, and with the finding that A-BTR compilation already draws on data scattered across multiple agencies and domains, assembling a report of this kind is a synthesis across all four stages rather than a lookup against one dataset, so every domain's pipeline has to be producing trustworthy data for the report to be assembled at all.
argument_units.warrant: Because A-BTR compilation requires all four adaptation-cycle pipelines to hold simultaneously, this is a data-platform-scale requirement covering ingestion, processing, and quality management across domains, not a single-service build; once that backend capability exists the public website follows as the audience-facing layer drawing on the same underlying material, rather than as a separate data problem.
argument_units.application_to_design: Name the four adaptation-cycle stages, explain why their pipelines and data quality must all hold for compilation to work, and state the data-platform conclusion directly. Do not frame this as a warning against an alternative -- no scaffolding of the form that the service would otherwise fail.

argument_units.claim: A service designed to close the A-BTR gap -- supplying the localized, Loss-and-Damage, outcome-indicator, and integration content the report names as missing, and the shared definitions and calculation methodology the pipeline needs, built on the cross-domain data platform this case establishes as necessary -- strengthens the general data platform and gives the public website real content to publish, so closing the most binding case also closes a meaningful share of the structural and content gaps established earlier in this section.
argument_units.grounds: Follows from the preceding units: the capabilities BTR2 names as missing (integrated databases, standardized outcome indicators), the capabilities the pipeline check names as missing (shared definitions, traceable calculation methodology), and the cross-domain platform the case requires are general-purpose data-platform capabilities that outlast A-BTR reporting alone. They close Gaps 5 and 10 directly, reach Gaps 1, 3, and 7 through the underlying data domains, and supply part of the website content shortfall stated at the start of this section.
argument_units.warrant: Because the same underlying capability -- an integrated, well-defined, traceable, cross-domain data system -- is what both the international reporting obligation and the general public platform require, investing to close the A-BTR gap is the same investment the platform needs regardless, applied first where the obligation is most binding.
argument_units.application_to_design: Close the section by stating the dual benefit directly and naming which structural gaps and which slice of the content gap this closes. Then point the reader to section 5.2 for the policy, technical, and governance recommendations that follow. Do not develop any recommendation here.
